approved: Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013
Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
The bill would re-establish a national regulator for the building and construction industry.
It would set up the Australian Building and Construction Commission to enforce workplace laws and the Building Code.
The government plans to move amendments clarifying the bill's application to offshore platforms and ships, and adding enforcement powers to the Building Code.
Re-establish the Australian Building and Construction Commission.
Clarify that building work includes transporting employees and contractors to building sites.
Add new matters to the Building Code for monitoring and enforcement.
Let the Building Code give the ABC Commissioner functions to enforce it.
Ensure code-authorized actions are not subject to coercion prohibitions in clause 54.
The building and construction industry, including employers, employees, and contractors on offshore resources platforms and ships.
Building and Construction Industry (Improving Productivity) Bill 2013 - Second Reading - Read a second time

Introduced a bill re-establishing the Australian Building and Construction Commission, abolished by Labor in 2012, citing a 2013 report finding the commission had lifted industry productivity by more than 9 per cent and saved consumers around $7.5 billion annually, and cited violent CFMEU disputes including threats at the Little Creatures Brewery site in Geelong.

Introduced a companion machinery bill to manage the transition from the Fair Work Building Industry Act 2012 to the newly re-established Australian Building and Construction Commission, and to deal with residual matters under the earlier Building and Construction Industry Improvement Act 2005.

Opposed the government's bill re-establishing the Australian Building and Construction Commission, arguing its coercive interview and imprisonment powers compromise civil liberties, and noted Fair Work Building and Construction had already recovered more than $2 million in unpaid wages for over 1,500 workers without such powers.

Opposed the ABCC bill, saying the earlier Cole royal commission spent $66 million over 18 months without securing a single criminal conviction, and said the ABCC had illegally interrogated about 203 people, calling the revived body an ABCC on steroids that extends into offshore construction and goods transport.

Supported the ABCC bill, citing a constituent's builder who lost more than $500,000 in work after refusing to sign a CFMEU enterprise agreement, and said a 2012 dispute over six underpaid workers cost the Queensland Children's Hospital project almost $100,000 a day during a weeks-long union picket.

Supported re-establishing the ABCC, citing his own earlier estimates that it delivered a 10 per cent productivity increase, a $5.5 billion annual welfare gain, and cut construction industry working days lost from 224 per 1,000 employees in 2004 to just 24 in 2006.

Opposed the ABCC bill, said the existing Fair Work Building and Construction regulator has already recovered over $2 million in unpaid entitlements for more than 1,500 workers, noted industrial disputation in construction is on average less than one-fifth the rate under the previous coalition government, and cited legal academics comparing the ABCC's coercive powers to those used in national security and terrorism law.

Supported the ABCC bill, said its sole purpose was to help deliver infrastructure projects on time and on budget, and cited the Cole royal commission's 2003 final report finding widespread disregard of laws and courts, threatening conduct and underpayment of workers' entitlements in the construction industry.

Opposed the ABCC bill on civil liberties grounds, arguing it denies equality before the law and the right to silence to construction workers alone, and noted the Cole royal commission, despite years of hearings and millions of dollars spent, resulted in zero prosecutions for the alleged criminal conduct it investigated.

Supported the ABCC bill, said the construction industry in his home city of Wagga Wagga, population 63,000, needs a strong watchdog after the previous government abolished the ABCC in February 2012, a decision he said was ill-conceived and made at the behest of minorities.

Supported the ABCC bill, cited a 2013 Independent Economics report finding the ABCC boosted construction productivity by more than nine per cent and benefited consumers by around $7.5 billion annually, and said its 2012 replacement faced a roughly 30 per cent cut to funding and staffing, with the new commission and code to commence on 1 January 2014.

Opposed the ABCC bill, said construction workplace fatalities peaked at 48 in 2006 and 51 in 2007 during the ABCC's most aggressive years, then fell to a decade-low of 30 after its 2012 abolition, and invoked the 1851 Chewton monster meeting of 15,000 miners as part of Australia's founding tradition of workers organising.

Supported the ABCC bill, said construction productivity grew 9.4 per cent under the original ABCC, working days lost to industrial disputes fell from an average of 159,000 a year before the ABCC to just 8,000 by the 2007 to 2008 year, then jumped from 24,000 to an estimated 89,000 between the 2011 to 2012 and 2012 to 2013 years after its abolition.

Opposed the ABCC bill, drawing on 25 years representing union members, described a workplace death his son witnessed on a WA construction site, noted the bill imposes penalties of $34,000 for individuals and $170,000 for organisations, and recalled the $70 million Cole royal commission producing not a single criminal charge.

Supported the ABCC bill, said it would benefit the 3,066 construction businesses in her Brisbane electorate, noted approximately 240,800 Queenslanders are employed in the construction industry, which represents around eight per cent of GDP, and said the re-established commission and code would commence on 1 January 2014.

Opposed the ABCC bill, said the $70 million Cole royal commission ran for a massive 1½ years without laying a single charge, noted the original ABCC cost taxpayers $250 million from 2005, and cited a case where 116 individual construction workers, not union leaders, faced fines exceeding $1 million.

Supported the ABCC bill, cited an Economist Intelligence Unit ranking placing Australia 50th of 51 countries for productivity growth in August 2012, said Labor left 200,000 more Australians unemployed after introducing or amending more than 21,000 regulations, and noted the ABCC previously delivered 9.4 per cent productivity growth and $7.5 billion in annual consumer benefits.

Opposed the ABCC bill, recounted construction worker Ark Tribe's two-year investigation and trial for refusing to attend a secret ABCC interview about a workplace safety meeting, and said the laws had been condemned by the International Labour Organization on eight separate occasions for undermining workers' rights to organise.

Supported the ABCC bill, said the original commission conducted over 400 investigations in the 2010 to 2011 year alone, uncovering more than 900 contraventions and $2.5 million in penalties, had a record of 74 successful prosecutions against only eight unsuccessful ones, and noted the CFMEU donated $1.7 million to the Labor Party in 2010 to 2011 alone.

Opposed the ABCC bill, said an independent fact-checker found the Prime Minister's election campaign claim that the ABCC delivered $6 billion a year in productivity savings to be largely unsubstantiated, and noted the Independent Economics report relied on by the government itself admits it cannot separately attribute productivity gains to the ABCC alone.

Opposed the bill to restore the Australian Building and Construction Commission, first established by the Howard government in 2005, drew on his own brothers' experiences in the building industry including a fatal crane collapse, and criticised the government for cutting $500 million from the automotive industry ahead of Holden's decision to leave Australia.

Opposed the ABCC bill, said almost 5,000 construction workers in his Charlton electorate would be affected, cited a construction fatality rate of 1.93 deaths per 100,000 workers under Labor's Fair Work model compared with a peak of 2.95 under the former ABCC, and noted the current inspectorate had already recovered $2 million in unpaid wages for more than 1,500 workers.

Opposed the ABCC bill, argued the current Fair Work Building and Construction regulator, established under legislation passed only around 18 months earlier in April 2012, has already recovered over $2 million in unpaid entitlements for more than 1,500 workers, more than the ABCC achieved when it operated between 2005 and 2012.

Opposed the ABCC bill, noting the Cole royal commission that preceded the ABCC's creation in 2005 cost $66 million over 18 months but produced no criminal convictions, and criticised the bill's reverse onus provisions and $34,000 maximum penalty for unlawful picketing as excessive and a breach of international labour conventions.
